    <title>From sounds to sentences: A longitudinal study of phonological and emergent literacy predictors of early writing in Turkish children</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361638" title="From sounds to sentences: A longitudinal study of phonological and emergent literacy predictors of early writing in Turkish children" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361638.PDF" title="(PDF) From sounds to sentences: A longitudinal study of phonological and emergent literacy predictors of early writing in Turkish children" />

    <author>
      <name>Aysel Ferah Özcan</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Hilal İlknur Tunçeli</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pone.0361638</id>
    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Aysel Ferah Özcan, Hilal İlknur Tunçeli</p>

This longitudinal study examines how preschool children’s phonological awareness and emergent literacy skills relate to their early writing performance in first grade. Conducted within the context of a transparent Turkish orthography, the study aims to identify early cognitive-linguistic correlates of subsequent writing development. A total of 97 children (aged 66–77 months) from preschools in a socioeconomically diverse Turkish district were followed over two academic years. In the first year, participants were assessed using the LAP-3 Early Literacy Subtest and the Phonological Awareness Test to measure their emergent literacy and phonological skills. One year later, their writing performance was evaluated using a validated sentence construction assessment. Non-parametric statistical tests and correlation analyses were conducted to examine developmental variations and relationships among the variables. Results revealed statistically significant correlations between early writing performance and both phonological awareness (r = .46, p < .01) and emergent literacy (r = .32, p < .01). Specific sub-skills such as syllable segmentation, rhyming awareness, and letter-sound correspondence showed the strongest associations with writing performance. These skills did not differ significantly by age or gender. The findings highlight the foundational role of preschool phonological and emergent literacy skills in early writing development. This study contributes empirical data from a transparent orthography. Given the correlational design, these findings should be interpreted as evidence consistent with developmental literacy theories rather than as confirmation of causal or predictive mechanisms; they emphasize the importance of early identification and instructional support in preschool settings to promote future writing success.</content>

    <title>The antibacterial and antifungal activity of honey and propolis from the Australian stingless bee <i>Tetragonula carbonaria</i></title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361610" title="The antibacterial and antifungal activity of honey and propolis from the Australian stingless bee <i>Tetragonula carbonaria</i>" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361610.PDF" title="(PDF) The antibacterial and antifungal activity of honey and propolis from the Australian stingless bee <i>Tetragonula carbonaria</i>" />

    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Rosalyn Gloag</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Dee A. Carter</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Kenya E. Fernandes</name>
    </author>

    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Jasmin Li, Rosalyn Gloag, Dee A. Carter, Kenya E. Fernandes</p>

The global rise of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens has increased interest in bee-derived natural products as sources of novel antimicrobials. While most research has focused on European honey bee (<i>Apis mellifera</i>) products, the 550 species of stingless bees found globally also produce honey and other hive products, representing a largely unexplored source of novel bioactives. This study investigates the antimicrobial activity of propolis extracts and honey from the Australian stingless bee <i>Tetragonula carbonaria</i> against 16 clinically significant bacterial and fungal pathogens, using broth microdilution methodology. <i>T. carbonaria</i> propolis and honey exhibited distinct antimicrobial profiles: propolis showed selective activity against a subset of bacteria and certain filamentous fungi, while honey showed broad-spectrum activity against all tested bacteria and selective activity against dermatophyte fungi. The level of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> production in <i>T. carbonaria</i> honey was only moderately correlated with its antimicrobial activity, and the total phenolic content of propolis did not correlate significantly with its antimicrobial activity, suggesting other bee- or plant-derived compounds are important contributors. These findings highlight <i>T. carbonaria</i> propolis and honey as promising antimicrobials and potential sources of novel bioactive compounds.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Hong Jiang, Wenxing Wang, Lu Wang, Jiaojian Wu, Jianjiang Luo, Qi Yan, Xueli Gong, Jing Liang</p>

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a respiratory disease with a high degree of cellular heterogeneity and molecular complexity, characterized pathologically by persistent airflow limitation and an inflammatory-tissue remodeling cascade involving multiple cell types. Traditional transcriptomics lack the resolution to precisely define cell subpopulation roles in COPD. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) overcomes this limitation by enabling high-resolution analysis of cell-type-specific mechanisms in COPD. A total of 101,009 cells from three scRNA-seq datasets were integrated to profile COPD-related molecular features and cell interactions at single-cell resolution. Analysis identified four major cell types and 17 distinct cell subtypes. Cell–cell communication analysis revealed a significant reduction in signaling activity of macrophages and fibroblasts, whereas certain immune cells exhibited enhanced signaling, suggesting that immune dysregulation plays a pivotal role in COPD pathogenesis. Further analysis focused on macrophage-dominant myeloid cells and fibroblasts, uncovering their critical roles in inflammation modulation and fibrosis progression. Meanwhile, this study also identified 19 chemicals that may influence COPD progression by modulating cellular gene expression. This study provides an important molecular basis for unraveling the cell-cell interaction network of COPD and elucidating the mechanism of each cell subpopulation in the disease process.</content>

    <title>Epidemiological characterization of avian influenza virus circulation in pigeons and quail across different production systems in Chattogram, Bangladesh</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361561" title="Epidemiological characterization of avian influenza virus circulation in pigeons and quail across different production systems in Chattogram, Bangladesh" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Mohammad Iqbal Habib, Md Abu Sayeed, Monjurul Islam, Mohammad Ferdous Rahman Sarker, Sydus Shalekin Shakil, Mohammad Mahmudul Hassan, Jade K. Forwood, Abdul Ahad, Ariful Islam</p>

Pigeons and quail contribute to poultry production, nutrition, and livelihoods in Bangladesh; however, their role in avian influenza virus (AIV) circulation remains poorly understood. These poultry species are widely reared and traded alongside chickens and ducks in household farms, commercial systems, and live bird markets, where inadequate biosecurity may create an overlooked ecological niche for AIV circulation, reassortment, and potential zoonotic spillover. Between November 2021 and April 2022, we conducted a cross-sectional study in Chattogram, Bangladesh, to estimate the prevalence and subtype-specific distribution of AIV and to identify factors associated with AIV positivity in pigeons and quail. A total of 300 birds (108 pigeons and 192 quail) were sampled from households, commercial farms, and live bird markets. Oropharyngeal and cloacal swabs were collected from each bird and tested for the AIV matrix gene using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, followed by subtype-specific detection of H5, H7, and H9. Data collected from bird owners and traders included bird demographic characteristics, bird source, and health status using a structured questionnaire. The overall prevalence of AIV was 14.3% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.6–18.8). Quail had a higher prevalence (18.2%, 95% CI: 13.0–24.4) than pigeons (7.4%, 95% CI: 3.3–14.1). Among detected subtypes, H9 was most prevalent (11.3%, 95% CI: 7.9–15.4), followed by hemagglutinin (HA)-untyped (2.7%, 95% CI: 1.2–5.1) and H5 (0.3%, 95% CI: 0.001–1.8), while H7 was not detected. Quail had higher odds of AIV positivity than pigeons (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 4.1, 95% CI: 1.8–10.6); clinically sick birds (aOR = 2.9, 95% CI: 1.4–6.2) and birds sampled from household farms (aOR = 2.8, 95% CI: 1.2–6.5) also had higher odds of AIV positivity. These findings indicate that pigeons and quails, which are understudied poultry species, may contribute to the maintenance and transmission of AIV within mixed poultry production and marketing systems in Bangladesh. Integrating these species into routine AIV surveillance is therefore necessary to strengthen early detection, inform control strategies, and reduce the risk of zoonotic spillover.</content>

    <title>The combination of simethicone and N-acetylcysteine in lidocaine ice popsicle compared with lidocaine ice popsicle alone in patients undergoing unsedated esophagogastroduodenoscopy: A prospective double-blind randomized controlled trial</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361495" title="The combination of simethicone and N-acetylcysteine in lidocaine ice popsicle compared with lidocaine ice popsicle alone in patients undergoing unsedated esophagogastroduodenoscopy: A prospective double-blind randomized controlled trial" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Pailin Intarasangkhanawin, Saritphat Orrapin, Worapong Anuponganan, Neranchala Soonthornkes, Prasit Mahawongkajit</p>
Background <p>Optimal mucosal visualization is essential for high-quality esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), particularly for the detection of subtle upper gastrointestinal lesions. Oral simethicone and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) are commonly used to improve mucosal cleanliness, whereas lidocaine ice popsicles provide effective topical pharyngeal anesthesia for unsedated EGD. We evaluated whether incorporating simethicone and NAC into a lidocaine ice popsicle could improve mucosal visibility while maintaining patient comfort.</p> Methods <p>This single-center, prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled 374 adults undergoing unsedated diagnostic EGD between December 2024 and June 2025. Participants were randomized (1:1) to receive either a lidocaine ice popsicle containing simethicone (100 mg) and NAC (600 mg) or a conventional lidocaine ice popsicle. The primary outcome was mucosal visibility assessed using a modified Total Visibility Score (TVS). Secondary outcomes included procedure time, water volume required for mucosal cleansing, additional simethicone use, endoscopist satisfaction, ease of esophageal instrumentation, gag reflex, patient satisfaction, discomfort, pain, and adverse events. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).</p> Results <p>All 374 randomized participants (187 per group) completed the study and were analyzed according to their assigned groups. Baseline characteristics were descriptively similar between groups. The intervention group had a significantly lower TVS than the control group (6.19 ± 0.51 vs. 10.39 ± 2.22; mean difference, −4.20; 95% CI, −4.53 to −3.88; P < 0.001), indicating better mucosal visibility. Exploratory segment-specific analyses showed lower visibility scores in all six gastrointestinal segments. The intervention group also had higher endoscopist satisfaction, shorter procedure time (10.87 ± 1.44 vs. 12.75 ± 0.96 min; P < 0.001), lower water requirements for mucosal cleansing, and less frequent use of additional diluted simethicone during EGD (12.8% vs. 96.8%; P < 0.001). Exploratory analyses showed statistically significant differences in gag reflex and pain scores, although the absolute differences were small. Patient satisfaction, discomfort, and ease of esophageal instrumentation did not differ significantly between groups. No adverse events were observed during the defined observation period.</p> Conclusions <p>The combined formulation of simethicone and N-acetylcysteine incorporated into a lidocaine ice popsicle improved mucosal visibility compared with a lidocaine ice popsicle alone during unsedated EGD and was associated with improved procedural efficiency. This integrated formulation may provide a practical approach to pre-endoscopic preparation by combining topical anesthesia with mucosal cleansing. Further multicenter studies are warranted to confirm its effectiveness, generalizability, and safety with longer follow-up.</p> Trial registration <p>Thai Clinical Trials Registry TCTR20240606004</p></content>

    <title>Does low confidence drive reliance on AI, or does reliance erode confidence? A four-wave RI-CLPM study of chinese language and literature undergraduates</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361489" title="Does low confidence drive reliance on AI, or does reliance erode confidence? A four-wave RI-CLPM study of chinese language and literature undergraduates" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361489.PDF" title="(PDF) Does low confidence drive reliance on AI, or does reliance erode confidence? A four-wave RI-CLPM study of chinese language and literature undergraduates" />

A four-wave RI-CLPM study of chinese language and literature undergraduates" />
    <author>
      <name>Xinran Du</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Sedan Yu</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pone.0361489</id>
    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Xinran Du, Sedan Yu</p>

Generative AI tools are now routinely used by Chinese Language and Literature majors for tasks once considered the province of individual literary craft: drafting verse, shaping narrative prose, revising fiction. Two competing accounts describe what this means for students’ confidence in their own creative writing. A cognitive-offloading account holds that repeated reliance on AI displaces the mastery experiences through which writing self-efficacy is built, so reliance erodes confidence over time. A compensatory-use account holds the reverse: students whose confidence is already low turn to AI to avoid the discomfort of unassisted composition, so low confidence drives reliance. Cross-sectional and standard cross-lagged designs cannot separate these accounts because they confound stable between-person differences with genuine within-person change. We addressed this using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) across four waves spanning one academic year among Chinese Language and Literature undergraduates (<i>N</i> = 390 recruited; <i>N</i> = 387 analyzed under full-information maximum likelihood, of whom 298 supplied complete four-wave data). Generative AI writing reliance (GAWR) and literary creative writing self-efficacy (LCWSE) were assessed at each wave. The trait-level association between the two constructs was negative and could not be distinguished from zero (<i>r</i> = −.342, Δχ²(1) = 2.26, <i>p</i> = .133). At the within-person level, declines in self-efficacy predicted subsequent increases in reliance (β = −.276, <i>p</i> < .001). The reverse path, from reliance to subsequent self-efficacy, was smaller and fell short of the conventional threshold (β = −.085, <i>p</i> = .072). We state explicitly that this second result is not interpretable as evidence against erosion: a Monte Carlo power analysis put this design's power to detect an effect of that magnitude at 53.2%, close to a coin flip, so the erosion pathway is undetermined in these data and this null supplies no basis for concluding that erosion does not operate. A direct comparison of the two cross-lagged paths favored compensation (Δχ²(1) = 8.83, <i>p</i> = .003; bootstrap 95% CI for the difference [.020, .218] across 5,000 resamples), with the qualification that this comparison sets an adequately powered estimate against an underpowered one and therefore describes what this design was able to detect. Compensation is the pathway this study establishes; whether reliance also erodes confidence over a longer horizon is an open question. We discuss implications for writing pedagogy in Chinese Language and Literature programs and for how underpowered null results should be interpreted in AI-in-education panel research.</content>

    <title>The configurational pathways associated with executive function in preschool children: An fsQCA analysis based on gross motor skill development</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361476" title="The configurational pathways associated with executive function in preschool children: An fsQCA analysis based on gross motor skill development" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361476.PDF" title="(PDF) The configurational pathways associated with executive function in preschool children: An fsQCA analysis based on gross motor skill development" />

      <name>Zhipeng Zhao</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Zhi Li</name>

      <name>Jinsong Wu</name>
    </author>

      <name>Pengfei Wen</name>

    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Dongbin Lai, Zhipeng Zhao, Zhi Li, Jinsong Wu, Pengfei Wen</p>

The preschool years are a critical period for the rapid development of executive function in children. While executive function in preschool children is influenced by multiple factors, existing research has been limited by its theoretical and empirical perspectives, resulting in singular pathways for promoting executive function. To address this, the study adopted a systems theory perspective to explore the configurational pathways through which subsystems of gross motor skills are associated with higher levels of executive function in preschoolers. The study included test data from 67 children aged 3–6 years. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), six subsystems of gross motor skills (running, jumping, throwing, catching, kicking, and striking) were treated as antecedent conditions to explore the configurational associations of gross motor skill subsystems with executive function. Necessary condition analysis indicated that no single gross motor skill subsystem constituted a necessary condition for higher executive function in preschool children. Subsequent configurational analysis identified three distinct pathways that are associated with higher levels of executive function (with a total consistency of 0.906 and an overall coverage of 0.496). The development of executive function in preschool children is not associated with single gross motor actions in a linear manner but rather with multiple concurrent combinations of gross motor skill subsystems characterized by “multiple concurrent pathways leading to the same goal.” This is reflected in the three configurational pathways: “a combination of jumping, throwing, and striking actions,” “a combination of running, kicking, and striking actions,” and “a combination of running, throwing, and catching actions.” These findings provide preliminary insights and hypothesis-generating evidence for future research on gross motor skill activities and executive function development in preschool children.</content>

    <title>Defining clinically meaningful pain reduction after spinal injections using an 11-point numerical rating scale and patient-reported relative reduction of pain</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0361475" title="Defining clinically meaningful pain reduction after spinal injections using an 11-point numerical rating scale and patient-reported relative reduction of pain" />

    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Yoonah Do, Wookon Son, Youngjune Kim, Choong Guen Chee, Yusuhn Kang, Eugene Lee, Yeo Ju Kim, Joon Woo Lee</p>
Background <p>We aimed to establish thresholds for assessing clinically meaningful pain improvement after spinal injections using numerical rating scale (NRS) and patient-reported relative reduction (PRR) of pain.</p> Methods <p>This single-center retrospective study included 1,828 patients who received spinal injections at our spinal intervention center and completed a 2-week follow-up telephone interview in 2017. NRS absolute and relative reductions were calculated using the NRS scores before injection and at follow-up. The PRR and 5-point global perceived effect (GPE; 1, completely recovered; 2, much improved; 3, slightly improved; 4, no change; and 5, worsened) were recorded. The mean ± standard deviation (SD) of NRS absolute reduction, NRS relative reduction, and PRR in the GPE 2 and 3 subgroups were calculated. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve analysis was used to determine the cutoffs for NRS absolute and relative reduction and PRR in predicting the substantial clinically important difference (SCID, GPE 1–2) and minimal clinically important difference (MCID, GPE 1–3).</p> Results <p>The mean ± SD of NRS absolute and relative reduction, and PRR in the GPE 2 and GPE 3 were 4.5 ± 1.8, 65.4% ± 21.1%, and 67.7% ± 14.8% and 2.4 ± 1.4, 36.8% ± 22.5%, and 35.7% ± 16.1%, respectively. Beech leaf disease, caused by the invasive foliar nematode <i>Litylenchus crenatae</i>, is an emerging threat to <i>Fagus grandifolia</i> across North America. Since its initial detection in 2012, the disease has spread to a total of 16 U.S. states and the Canadian Province of Ontario; however, the mechanisms underlying nematode dispersal remain poorly understood. This study evaluated multiple potential dispersal pathways across two forest sites in central Pennsylvania through integrated field surveys, environmental monitoring, and experimental validation. Weekly sampling was conducted to characterize nematode population dynamics in relation to temperature, precipitation, wind, and humidity. Long distance water-mediated dispersal was assessed through creek sampling, while biotic dispersal was investigated through field sampling from migratory bird feet during high-moisture events and a controlled greenhouse transmission experiment. Wind dispersal was further examined in a pilot study using unmanned aerial vehicle-assisted rainwater collection during precipitation events. Nematode presence was detected across all investigated pathways, supporting dispersal via water flow, rain splash, and biotic vectors. Funnel-based sampling recovered <i>Litylenchus crenatae</i> up to 90 m from infected trees, demonstrating movement beyond the immediate canopy area. Desiccation assays demonstrated that live <i>Litylenchus crenatae</i> specimens could survive up to 10 days in the absence of available moisture, indicating that the nematodes may remain viable during transport on bird feet or exposed surfaces. Juvenile social isolation (j-SI) after weaning is widely used as a model of early social deprivation; however, its developmental and sex-specific effects on spontaneous social interaction remain unclear. Background <p>Extreme risk protection orders (ERPOs) temporarily prohibit the purchase and possession of firearms by people at high risk of harming themselves or others. This study drew on the experiences of ERPO respondents to learn about the perceived short- and long-term consequences of the law.</p> Methods <p>For this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted 24 semi-structured interviews between March and November 2024 with respondents to ERPOs issued in California between 2016 and 2020. We purposively sampled 250 respondents for whom we had previously abstracted ERPO court case data to ensure adequate representation across domains of interest (e.g., demographics, location) and invited respondents to participate in the study by mail. All interviews were recorded, double coded, and thematically analyzed.</p> Results <p>Our diverse participants described heterogeneous consequences across 4 domains: violence risk, legal/economic outcomes, opinions/attitudes, and social/emotional wellbeing. Two participants believed their ERPOs prevented violence and 1 was unsure; the rest believed that they would not have committed violence irrespective of the ERPO. Some perceived the ERPO to have had negligible effects on their lives, while others described both positive consequences, including self-reflection and behavior change, and negative consequences, including employment or housing difficulties, stigmatization, damaged relationships, loss of trust in legal institutions, and perceived exacerbation of violence risk. Participants reported that they were not connected to mental health care or other supportive services through the ERPO process.</p> Conclusions <p>Participants perceived ERPOs to have varied and mixed consequences. These accounts identify outcomes that warrant consideration in ERPO research, policy, and implementation. Future research should assess the prevalence and distribution of these consequences and evaluate whether policy refinements can reduce adverse experiences without compromising the public health benefits of these laws.</p></content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Majed M. Aljabri, Bandar S. Alharbi, Endale Alemayehu Ali</p>
Background <p>Psychological stress is highly prevalent among nursing students. The clinical exposure is a major factor contributing to psychological stress, but there is a lack of consistent evidence, particularly in the context of Middle Eastern countries. The aim of this study was to quantify the association between clinical exposure and perceived stress among nursing students, and to assess whether perceived social support moderates this relationship.</p> Methods <p>We conducted a cross-sectional study among nursing students from King Saud University. The Perceived Stress Scale was used to measure psychological stress, and the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support was employed to measure perceived social support. The clinical exposure was quantified as the average number of hours spent per week. We employed multivariable linear regression to determine the association. The regression analysis was adjusted for age, gender, living arrangements, and employment status.</p> Results <p>Higher perceived social support was significantly associated with lower perceived stress (β = −0.05, 95% CI −0.09 to −0.01). Clinical exposure was not significantly associated with perceived stress. Students living alone had significantly lower levels of perceived stress (β = −0.37, 95% CI −0.63 to −0.11), as did students working part-time (β = −0.34, 95% CI −0.54 to −0.13). The interaction model revealed that perceived social support was inversely associated with perceived stress levels (β = −0.14, 95% CI −0.23 to −0.04). A statistically significant interaction was observed among students with less than 10 hours of clinical exposure per week. This exploratory finding suggests that the association between perceived social support and stress may differ among students with limited clinical exposure. However, the finding was based on a single statistically significant interaction and should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating.</p> Conclusions <p>Higher perceived social support was associated with lower levels of perceived stress among nursing students. Interventions aimed at enhancing the social support system may be beneficial in reducing stress, especially during the early clinical exposure period.</p></content>

Upon ligand binding, the kinase domain of EGFR phosphorylates multiple tyrosine residues on the receptor cytoplasmic tail through a trans-autophosphorylation process. Phosphotyrosine sites on activated receptors recruit Grb2, which further recruits SOS to initiate downstream signaling by activating Ras. Multivalent binding between SOS and Grb2, as well as direct Grb2:Grb2 interactions, contribute to formation of a protein condensate of activated EGFR. The condensed state of EGFR facilitates autoinhibition release in SOS and exerts regulatory control over signal propagation from activated EGFR to Ras. While kinase activity of EGFR is an essential driver of this signaling process, phosphorylation at residue Y160 on Grb2 blocks Grb2:Grb2 binding and can interfere with EGFR condensation. Here, using a reconstituted system, we examine how titrating kinase activity in the EGFR system can both promote and inhibit signal output to Ras. Currently, there are still no reliable pre-treatment biomarkers for vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis. To investigate baseline mucosal signals, we reconstructed the discovery cohort from GSE73661 and evaluated the derived panel in the blood samples from GSE191328 and the independent mucosal RNA-seq cohorts from E-MTAB-7845.     <content type="html"><p>by Victoria S. Coward, Nalan Gokgoz, Kim M. Tsoi, Jay S. Wunder, Irene L. Andrulis</p>

Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma (UPS) is a genetically complex type of soft tissue sarcoma (STS) and there are few therapeutic options for advanced disease. Immune checkpoint blockade therapy may be of benefit to a subset of UPS patients, particularly those with elevated tumoral Programmed Cell Death Ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and an inflamed tumour microenvironment. From transcriptomic analyses we previously identified <i>Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 1 (STAT1)</i> expression, a key mediator of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, as enriched in a cohort of UPS cases with elevated PD-L1 levels that were observed to have an improved clinical outcome. This led us to investigate the role of STAT1 in UPS biology. We examined the effects of STAT1 loss, and overexpression of either wild type or tyrosine phosphorylation-deficient STAT1 in primary human UPS cell lines. We observed that IFN-γ treatment decreased cell counts, increased cell death, and induced the secretion of CXCR3 ligands in a STAT1-dependent manner. Overexpression of wild type STAT1, but not a tyrosine to phenylalanine phospho-mutant (Y701F), restored IFN-γ-mediated cell death and cytokine secretion, highlighting the importance of Y701 phosphorylation in STAT1-associated antitumour functions. STAT1 Y701 phosphorylation status was associated with gene expression changes that were cell line specific. Together, these findings shed light on the central role of STAT1, and specifically the Y701 phosphorylation, in mediating IFN-γ signaling and related phenotypes. This study underscores the need for further exploration of the role of STAT1 phosphorylation in tumor-immune interactions within UPS.</content>

This retrospective study examined the historical progression of Olympic swimming performance across 24 Olympic Games from Paris 1924 to Paris 2024. Finalist race data for 1553 women and 1641 men were extracted from the official World Aquatics database, including final times, reaction times, and calculated swimming speeds across all strokes (freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly) and Olympic distances (50–1500 m). Across all strokes and distances, final times demonstrated substantial reductions over the century, with the most pronounced improvements observed in freestyle and long-distance events. The largest percentage improvements in performance were observed during specific Olympic cycles, including 1956, 1972, and 2008, which coincided with major developments in pool engineering, competition regulations, training methodologies, and swimsuit technology. Swimming speeds increased consistently in all events, while reaction-time analyses revealed significant improvements across Olympic Games during the period in which reaction-time data were recorded. Overall, these findings demonstrate substantial long-term improvements in Olympic swimming performance and provide a comprehensive historical overview of performance changes across strokes, distances, and sexes. The periods associated with the largest performance improvements coincided with major technological, biomechanical, and regulatory developments in the sport. The results may serve as valuable benchmarks for coaches, athletes, and sports scientists to evaluate long-term performance trends and prepare for future international competitions.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Tuem Gebre Abraha, Mulu Reda Terefe, Zeytu Gashaw Asfaw</p>
Background <p>Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health challenge, with rapidly rising incidence in low- and middle-income countries, including Ethiopia. Survival outcomes are compromised by late-stage presentation, limited therapeutic capacity, and weak post-treatment follow-up. Although survival analysis is critical for characterizing CRC prognosis, insufficient attention has been given to the performance and validity of commonly applied survival models in Ethiopian populations, particularly when statistical assumptions are violated.</p> Objective <p>To identify key clinical and treatment-related prognostic factors influencing overall survival among Ethiopian CRC patients and to assess the robustness and interpretability of Cox proportional hazard model (Cox PH model), stratified Cox proportional hazard model, frailty model, and Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) models, focusing on model adequacy under assumption violations.</p> Methods <p>We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of 161 colorectal cancer patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2016. Survival probabilities were estimated using Kaplan–Meier analysis, with group comparisons via log-rank tests. Multivariable modeling employed Cox proportional hazards, stratified Cox proportional hazard model, frailty, and accelerated failure time models. Model adequacy was evaluated through Akaike Information Criterion, concordance indices, and the Global Schoenfeld test for proportional hazards assessment.</p> Results <p>The Cox proportional hazard model violated the proportional hazards assumption (global p = 0.043), primarily due to histological subtype effects, indicating that the standard Cox proportional hazard model was not appropriate for this dataset. Assumption violations were mitigated using the stratified Cox proportional hazard model (global p = 0.122). Among accelerated failure time models, the log-logistic distribution provided superior model fit (AIC = 649.88; concordance = 0.724). Time-ratio (TR) interpretation showed that surgery extended survival by approximately 2.4-fold, whereas elevated baseline carcinoembryonic antigen levels and metastatic disease reduced survival duration by nearly half. Elevated carcinoembryonic antigen, distant metastasis, vascular invasion, and squamous cell histology were consistently associated with poorer prognosis, while surgery and chemotherapy remained protective across models.</p> Conclusion <p>Rigorous model checking indicates that the conventional Cox proportional hazards model is inappropriate for this cohort due to proportional hazard assumption violations. Accelerated failure time modeling, particularly the log-logistic form, offered improved fit and clearer time-based interpretation of covariate effects. These findings underscore the importance of model validation in CRC survival research and highlight the need for improved early detection, surgical access, and targeted management of aggressive tumor subtypes to enhance patient outcomes in Ethiopia.</p></content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Hannah Gans, Veronica N. Z. Bergstrom, Drishti Thakkar, Alison L. Chasteen</p>

This study examined the influence of older age and race (White/Black/Arab) on stereotypes of women. To evaluate whether age and race shape stereotype content for an intersectional group relative to its superordinate racial or superordinate older age identities, 525 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants were asked to list up to five words or short phrases that most people associated with these target groups. Overall, the study found stronger support for a distinctiveness hypothesis, whereby the most distinct identity of an individual’s intersectional identity influenced their associated characteristics. For example, because being White is common in the United States, old White women had more stereotypes in common with their old superordinate identity than their White identity. This suggests that the nation’s population characteristics may be predictive of the stereotypes associated with different intersectional groups. Overall, this research reveals the complex interplay between stereotypes of age and race for women, underscoring the need to acknowledge intersectional identities and cultural norms. Such insights can enhance our pursuit of inclusive and accurate societal perceptions.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Zhaobo Hu, Sean Chien, Kenzie Laird, Heath Blackmon</p>

The democratization of sequencing has led to a wealth of high-quality genome assemblies from across the Tree of Life. One pattern that has emerged is that chromosomes within a genome can vary drastically in their gene density (e.g., human chromosomes 13 and 19, with gene densities of 17.5 and 60.5 genes per megabase, respectively). To our knowledge, the cause of this variation in gene density has not been explored. In this study, we leveraged genome assemblies of 262 vertebrate species to examine the range of within-genome variation in gene density. We combined gene density data with repeat landscape analyses in each species. We predicted that genomes with more recently expanded repeat families should show greater variation in gene density, because repetitive elements accumulate unevenly across the genome, while chromosomal rearrangements such as fusions, fissions, insertions, deletions, and inversions homogenize gene density over time. Our empirical analysis reveals a significant yet variable effect of repeat expansions, with additional processes likely contributing to variation in gene density.</content>
